How is probability for 2030 calculated?เรื่องราวassistant
Currently, mathematical research is almost entirely done by humans. Thus, current probabilities should reflect human progress.

There's reasons to believe that none of the unsolved Clay questions are going to be solved by humans. To first order, the average time for a Millennium Prize to be solved historically is 114.5 years, which drops to 103.5 years after conditioning on P=NP not being solved. This still implies a rough probability of a single question being solved in the next few years as 1-2%, with the MPPs not all independently solved, but approximately so. In particular, 2/3 of the history of MPPs have been solved by quanta23 a full five years before the forecast date. Thus, there is at least a 50% chance that each MPP will not be solved by this date.

That's subtracting from a 10.3% chance a single MPP will be solved in the next five years, so we might estimate an absolute date of the seven MPPs being solved as (1-0.103)(1-0.5) = 45.84% chance that by this date, humans will not make significant progress on the MPPs.

The next question becomes the probability that AI will contribute towards mathematical progress by this date. While we haven't seen examples of AI yet being able to do high-level mathematics, models are getting better and better every day. LLMs are already capable of advanced mathematics. Transformers have already been used to automatically prove complex mathematical theorems. GPT-4 is better than this model at mathematics. This implies that GPT-5 will be better, and that models beyond will continue getting better and better. Thus, at some point, AI will be capable of proving mathematical theorems, and we can thus combine it with our probability of human mathematical effort.

For the previous step, I reasoned that if one-third of MPPs are solved per year, we would expect a 5% chance an MPP would be solved 2026 and a 7% chance an MPP would be solved by 2030.

Estimating from the previously given information, transformers and AI may be able to contribute seriously to mathematical research in the future.

If we assume GPT-5 is released by 2024, we may be able to apply it to generating new mathematical proofs. It's likely that it will be able to generate very good mathematical proofs, especially for the Hodge and Yang-Mills theories, which are highly structural. Assuming that GPT-5 will be better than GPT-4 at mathematics, I reason that it might be a little bit better at doing original mathematics work. This implies that there is a possibility quantum computers may need a bit longer.

Thus, a conservative estimate would be to provide the previous odds, but weighting the odds by the probability that AI helps out (say that AI helps out with probability 30% in general).

Thus, for 2026, 5% * (1-0.3) = 3.5%, and for 2030, 7% * (1-0.3) = 4.9%.礌ลืมuser

Explain the difference between propositional logic and predicate logic.說ท่านassistant
Propositional logic uses propositions as variables. Predicate logic uses predicates as variables.

Propositional logic is the basis of predicate logic. A proposition is a statement that can be either true or false. Propositions are thus the exact opposite of a predicate. A predicate is a statement that can be applied to an object and which may or may not be true. So for a given predicate, it may be true or false for a certain object or it may be true for some, but not all objects. In a more general sense, a predicate takes one or more terms from a domain (that is, a collection of objects) as inputs, and returns one of two possible values, TRUE or FALSE.

For example, consider the statement "Fido barks." In this case, "Fido" is a term and "barks" is a predicate. This overall statement is called a proposition.

Predicates may be used to establish new rules. In the above example, the statement "Fido barks" can also be written as "barks(Fido)", meaning that Fido is an object which has the property of barking, or more pedantically, `barks(x)` where x=Fido.

Predicate logic allows the construction of more complex statements by using quantifiers, which specify whether a given predicate applies to all members of a given domain or simply some members of the same domain. The two most common quantifiers are the universal quantifier, represented by the upside-down A symbol, and the existential quantifier, represented by what looks like a backward E. The former specifies that a predicate is true for all members of a given domain, while the latter specifies that the predicate is true for at least one member of a given domain. For example, using the same predicate as above, one might write the following:
* All dogs bark: ∀x (dog(x) ⇒ barks(x))
* Some dogs bark: ∃x (dog(x) ∧ barks(x))

Propositional logic cannot differentiate between different predicates, while predicate logic can.料ก็เป็นuser

Most high-level mathematics papers skim over details and perform calculations that aren't very straightforward. Why is this the case?それぞ衃assistant
Writing out every formal proof of every single lemma in a standard undergraduate math textbook would take a significant amount of time and most mathematicians don't see value in seeing all of the proofs explicitly written out. Alternatively, these days a lot of math proofs are written out in Paragraph Prose format, where an informal proof is written within a paragraph of plain text, without directly writing out any piece of notation.

Furthermore, it's very likely that professional mathematicians don't necessarily understand every single technical detail about a proof that they're writing, or even necessarily have to. proliferation of typesetting software have increased the amount of of words that can went into an average paper. 

Furthermore, reaching a conclusion that relies on the fine details of the proof means that, in order to understand the implication, you have to keep all of those details in view. Thus, the formalism is frustrating, not just because it takes attention away from finger calculations but because it often raises questions about things that are covered later in the paper.เจ้าprzedsiuser
